title: Web Design
summary: Building web pages with HTML: how websites work, page structure, the tags you use, and styling with CSS.
learn: What HTML is, and the first website
Good and bad website design, and navigation
How a browser knows what to display
intro: How the web began, what makes a website well or badly designed, and how to build your own pages with HTML tags, links, a navbar and CSS styling.

pages.spec: Describe the internet, the World Wide Web and how the first website was made
pages.summary: The internet is the hardware network; the World Wide Web is the collection of websites on it. Tim Berners-Lee made the first website on 6 August 1991 using HTML.

blocks.text: The starter puzzle showed a jumble of text full of angle brackets like `<TITLE>` and `<A HREF=…>`. It is the code of the **very first website**. Your browser turns code like this into the pages you see.
Key terms

head: Key term
Meaning
rows: A global network of interconnected computers. It is the **hardware**: the computers, cables and wireless links that communicate with one another.
A huge collection of websites that we access through the internet. It holds web pages and web resources such as images and videos. It is the **software/content** hosted on the internet.
Each website has multiple screens, each one called a web page.
A word or image you click to take you to another web page.
A program that reads and displays HTML documents, e.g. Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge. It does not show the HTML tags but uses them to display the page.
The unique address of a web page, e.g. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news.
blocks.caption: Key terms used in websites

blocks.text: The internet and the World Wide Web are **not** the same thing. Email and online gaming use the internet but are not part of the web.
The first website

The first website went live on **6 August 1991**. It was made by **Tim Berners-Lee**, a British computer scientist working at CERN, a science laboratory in Switzerland. He saw a huge demand for universities around the world to share information automatically.

items: **1989** – Berners-Lee starts the World Wide Web project.
He writes the rules for **HTTP** (how pages are sent) and **HTML** (how pages are written), so every computer shares pages the same way.
**1991** – the first website goes live.
**1994** – he founds the **World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)**, which sets web standards and helped the web grow into social media, online shopping and streaming.

blocks.title: first-site.html (tidied up into modern HTML)
blocks.code:
World Wide Web

The WorldWideWeb (W3) is a wide-area hypermedia information retrieval initiative aiming to give universal access to a large universe of documents.
blocks.output: A large heading ‘World Wide Web’, then a paragraph with the word ‘hypermedia’ as a clickable link.

blocks.text: It might not look like much, but this was not just a Word document: it could be opened and read by anyone, anywhere in the world, and linked to other pages. That is what made it revolutionary.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Internet = hardware network; WWW = websites hosted on it.
A website is made of web pages linked by hyperlinks.
A browser reads HTML and displays the page.
Tim Berners-Lee made the first website on 6 August 1991.
He founded the W3C in 1994.

pages.spec: Identify common website design mistakes and how to fix them
pages.summary: Bad websites use too many colours and fonts, are hard to navigate and read, and have unclear pictures. Good websites are clean, consistent, readable, with clear images and a 3–5 colour scheme.

blocks.text: Websites differ in their fonts, colours and interactive features. When building one it is easy to get carried away, and your site ends up looking a mess. The usual problems are:

items: Colour schemes with too many colours
Layout that is hard to navigate
Text that is difficult to read
Eyes drawn all over the place, with no order to where you should look
Pictures that are not clear (pixelated)
No alignment of text and text boxes

blocks.text: Spot the mistakes: the ‘worst website’ example

head: Mistake on the example site
Why it is bad / the fix
rows: Too many fonts, including Brush Script and Word Art; some not web-safe
Looks messy and may not display on every computer. Use one or two clear fonts.
Blue on red, red on blue, blue or red on black
Very hard to read. Use strong contrast, e.g. dark text on a light background.
Distracting and unprofessional. Keep backgrounds plain.
Animated stars, flashing ‘New’ icons, animated email icons, scrolling text
Pull your eyes everywhere. Use animation rarely, if at all.
‘Under construction’ notices, page counter, ‘last updated’ script
Make the site look unfinished. Leave them off.
Spellings like ‘kewl’, ‘u’, ‘1’, and words like ‘sight’ for ‘site’
Inconsistent menu, a link that does not work, link text that does not match the page title
Confuses users. Test every link and keep the menu identical on every page.
Mouse-over that makes text bigger or bold
The layout jumps. Change colour only.
A big photo shrunk with HTML; a small photo stretched bigger
The first is a huge slow download; the second is pixelated. Resize images properly before uploading.
Sunset photo saved as a GIF
GIFs only have 256 colours, so photos look grainy. Use JPEG for photos.
Cannot be searched or read by screen readers. Use real HTML text.
Table too wide, causing a horizontal scrollbar; text touching borders
Fit the page to the screen and add padding.
Background music that loops forever and cannot be turned off
Very annoying. Avoid sound, or give a quick way to turn it off.
Poor file naming. Give files meaningful names, e.g. hobbies.html.
blocks.caption: Some of the things wrong with a deliberately bad website

blocks.text: How to fix most of these

items: Keep your website **clean and clear** (balanced).
Make the **navigation** easy to use.
Keep your **page layout consistent**.
Make images **clear, appropriate and a suitable size**.
Make text **readable and consistent**.
Use a well-thought-out **colour scheme of 3–5 colours**.

blocks.text: Test your site by asking someone else, e.g. a younger sibling, to find a page on it. If they get lost, your navigation needs work.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Too many colours and fonts make a site hard to use.
Use a 3–5 colour scheme and readable, consistent text.
Keep the layout and menu consistent on every page.
Images must be clear and correctly sized.
Avoid flashing, animated or noisy extras.

check.q: How many colours should a good website colour scheme usually have?
check.why: 3–5 colours keeps a site clear and consistent.

check.q: Why is red text on a blue background a bad idea?
o: It is very hard to read
It makes the page load slowly
check.why: Poor contrast makes text difficult to read.

check.q: A small photo has been stretched to fill the page. What will it look like?
check.why: Enlarging a small bitmap makes it pixelated.

check.q: Which of these is good design?
o: The same menu on every page
check.why: Consistent navigation is good design.

practice.q: State **three** common problems with badly designed websites.
practice.a: Any three: too many colours (1); hard to navigate (1); text hard to read (1); eyes drawn all over the place (1); pictures not clear/pixelated (1); no alignment of text (1).

practice.q: Give **three** ways to make a website well designed.
practice.a: Any three: clean and clear layout (1); easy navigation (1); consistent layout (1); clear, suitably sized images (1); readable, consistent text (1); 3–5 colour scheme (1).

pages.spec: Explain why good navigation matters and describe features of a good navigation bar
pages.summary: Users leave sites that are hard to navigate. A good menu is the same on every page, clearly identifiable, with clearly named buttons and subtle rollover effects.

blocks.text: [[Navigation]] means how users move around a website. It is a key part of design and must be easy for your **target audience** (the people the site is made for) to use.
Research shows users will simply leave a website if it is difficult to navigate. Think how quickly you give up on a slow, confusing app.
Rules for good navigation

items: **Consistency** in menus and buttons is super important.
The **menu should be the same on every page** of the website.
The **main menu should be clearly identifiable**.
Each button (hyperlink) should be **clearly named**, so the user knows exactly what to expect when they press it.
**Rollover effects** on buttons (e.g. changing colour when the mouse is over them) add interactivity, as long as they do not distract the user.

blocks.text: What do navigation bars have in common?
Look at the navigation bars of Facebook, X (Twitter), Apple and Google. They use very different colour schemes but share very similar qualities:

head: Similarity
Why
rows: A horizontal bar across the top of the page
Where users expect to look first
Logo or site name at the left
Shows whose site it is; often links back to the home page
Short, clear one- or two-word labels (Home, Profile, Store)
Users know where each link goes
Same position and style on every page
Strong contrast between bar and text
Current page or hovered link highlighted

blocks.title: Worked example: which sites follow the rules?
blocks.context: Think of other websites. Do they follow these rules?
steps: BBC Bitesize: bar along the top, logo on the left, clear subject links, the same on every page – follows the rules.
Amazon: logo on the left, search in the middle, account and basket on the right on every page – follows the rules.
A site where the menu moves around or uses unlabelled icons only – breaks the rules, because users cannot predict where links go.
blocks.answer: Most big, successful sites follow the same navigation rules because users expect them.

blocks.text: Label buttons with what the user gets (‘Fixtures’, ‘Contact us’), not clever names (‘The Zone’). Nobody clicks a mystery button.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Navigation = how users move around a site.
Users leave sites that are hard to navigate.
Keep the menu the same on every page and easy to spot.
Name every button clearly.
Rollover effects are fine if they do not distract.

check.q: Why is navigation so important?
o: It makes the site load faster
Users will leave a website that is hard to navigate
check.why: Research shows people abandon hard-to-navigate sites.

check.q: Where should the main menu appear?
o: In the same place on every page
In a different place on each page
check.why: Consistency means the same menu on every page.

check.q: What is a rollover effect?
o: A page that scrolls by itself
A button that changes when the mouse moves over it
check.why: Rollovers react to the mouse pointer.

practice.q: Describe **three** features of good website navigation.
practice.a: Menu is the same/consistent on every page (1); main menu is clearly identifiable (1); buttons clearly named so user knows where they go (1); rollover effects that do not distract (1). Any three.

practice.q: Explain why a website designer should keep the menu consistent on every page.
practice.a: Users always know where to find the menu/links (1) so they do not get lost or confused and leave the site (1).

pages.spec: Explain what HTML is and how tags, closing tags and attributes work
pages.summary: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags in angle brackets to label content. Tags usually come in pairs; the closing tag has a forward slash. Tags can have attributes and can be nested.

blocks.text: [[HTML]] stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. It is the language used to create web pages on the World Wide Web. It describes the **content** and **structure** of a page. The latest version is **HTML5**.

Web developers (the people who make websites) do not make websites in Microsoft Word or by dragging boxes around in a website builder like Wix. Even a big site like Miniclip is really made of HTML tags that you never see.

When you visit a website, your browser loads a **plain text file** full of tags. The browser ‘reads’ the tags and draws the headings, images and buttons. It is like reading a book: the page is only words, but your imagination creates the pictures. With websites, the browser creates the picture.
It is not as complicated as it looks!

items: **Tags** are used throughout an HTML document.
Tags use **angled brackets**: `<` and `>`.
Tags nearly always come in **pairs**. If you open a tag you must close it. The closing tag has a **forward slash** `/`.
Tags can have **attributes** that change their appearance or what they do.
Tags can be **embedded (nested)** inside each other.

blocks.title: Nesting: the title tag is inside the head tag

head: Line
What is happening
rows: The title tag is opened and closed **inside** the head tag

blocks.text: Anatomy of an element
An [[element]] is an opening tag, some content, and a closing tag:

blocks.title: The pattern for most tags
blocks.code: <tagname>Content to be displayed can go here…</tagname>

items: `<tagname>` – the **starting (opening) tag**, surrounded by angled brackets.
The content between the tags is what is actually displayed on screen.
`</tagname>` – the **closing tag**: just like the opening tag but with a forward slash before the name.

blocks.text:
Close tags in the reverse order you opened them: `

Hi

` is right; `

Hi

` is wrong.

blocks.title: Key points
items: HTML = HyperText Markup Language; latest version HTML5.
A web page is a text file of tags that the browser reads.
Tags use < and >, usually in pairs; closing tags have /.
Attributes go inside the opening tag.
Tags can be nested inside each other.

check.q: What does HTML stand for?
check.why: HyperText Markup Language.

check.q: Which is a correct closing tag?
check.why: The closing tag puts a forward slash before the tag name.

check.q: What is the latest version of HTML?
check.why: HTML5.

check.q: In `<head><title>Hi</title></head>`, which tag is nested inside which?
check.why: The title opens and closes inside the head.

practice.q: Explain what HTML is and how a browser uses it.
practice.a: HTML is HyperText Markup Language, the language used to create web pages (1). A web page is a text file of tags (1). The browser reads/interprets the tags and displays the content without showing the tags (1).

practice.q: State **three** rules about HTML tags.
practice.a: Use angled brackets < > (1); usually come in pairs / must be closed (1); closing tag has a forward slash (1); can have attributes (1); can be nested (1). Any three.

pages.spec: Describe the structure of an HTML page and what each main tag does
pages.summary: Every page has <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html> containing a <head> (information for the browser, including the <title>) and a <body> (everything visible).

blocks.text: HTML tags label pieces of content such as a ‘heading’, ‘paragraph’ or ‘table’. Browsers do not display the tags; they use them to render (draw) the content. Here is a very simple HTML file:

blocks.title: index.html
blocks.code:
My First Heading

My first paragraph.
blocks.output: The browser tab says ‘Page Title’. The page shows a big bold heading ‘My First Heading’ and below it the text ‘My first paragraph.’

head: Tag
What it does
rows: Declares the document is HTML5, so the browser knows it is a web page.
The **root element**. EVERY other tag goes inside it; it tells the browser this is the website content.
Holds **meta information** about the page: things the browser needs to know but that do not appear on the page itself.
The title of the page, shown in the browser **tab**.
Contains all the **visible** content of the page.
‘Heading 1’, a large heading. There are smaller ones: `<h2>`, `<h3>` … `<h6>`.
blocks.caption: The key tags in a simple page

blocks.text: Indenting your code

Use the **Tab** key to indent nested tags. If a tag is ‘inside’ another, tab it in. This makes it very clear what is inside what. Above, the `

` and `

` are inside `` because they both start and end inside it.
What is displayed?
Only what is inside the `<body>` is shown on the page (plus the `<title>`, in the tab). The other tags must still be there because the browser uses them.
All content you want to display must go inside `<body>`. Text typed into the `<head>` will not appear properly on the page.
Think of a person: the **head** holds information you cannot see (thoughts), the **body** is what everyone sees.

blocks.title: Key points
items: <!DOCTYPE html> says ‘this is HTML5’.
<html> is the root element: everything goes inside it.
<head> holds information for the browser; <title> appears in the tab.
<body> holds everything visible.
Indent nested tags with Tab to keep code readable.

diagram.title: Structure of an HTML page
diagram.caption: Each box sits inside the one above it.

items.label: <!DOCTYPE html>
items.detail: First line: this is an HTML5 document.

items.label: <head> … </head>
items.detail: Information for the browser, including <title> (shown in the tab). Not displayed on the page.

items.label: <body> … </body>
items.detail: Everything the user sees: headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists.

pages.spec: Create hyperlinks between pages and organise website files into folders
pages.summary: Links use the anchor tag <a> with an href attribute giving the destination. Pages in the same folder link by file name; pages in a subfolder need the folder name in the path.

blocks.text: HTML links (hyperlinks) are made with the **anchor** tag, `<a>`. It uses the [[href]] attribute, inside the opening tag, to say where the link goes.

blocks.title: A link to Google
blocks.code: Click Here to go to Google
blocks.output: The words ‘Click Here to go to Google’ appear as a clickable link.

items: `<a …>` is the opening tag.
`href="…"` is the **destination**: where you go when you click. It is not displayed.
The text between the tags is what you see and click on.
`` is the closing tag.

blocks.text: Setting up folders for a full website

items: Open your **Year 9** folder, then your **ICT** folder.
Create a subfolder called **HTML** (if you have not already).
Inside it create a folder called **MyWebsite**.
Make two HTML files inside MyWebsite: **Index.html** and **Hobbies.html**.
Check with the person beside you that the files really end in .html (not .html.txt).

blocks.text: **Index.html** is the [[home page]]: it is universally treated as the first page of a website, and web servers open it automatically.

blocks.title: MyWebsite/Index.html
blocks.code:
This is going to be your homepage of your website

My hobbies Link to Contact page Click Here to go to Google

blocks.title: MyWebsite/Hobbies.html
blocks.code:
This is going to be your Hobby page

Back to Home

blocks.text: Absolute and relative links

head: Link to another website
Link to a page in your site
rows: A relative link (where the file is compared with this page)
Same folder: just the file name

blocks.text: Because Index.html and Hobbies.html are in the **same folder** (MyWebsite), the link only needs `Hobbies.html`, not a full path like `C:/HTML/Hobbies.html`. If contact.html is in a subfolder called **Contact** inside MyWebsite, you tell the browser where it is compared with your index page: `Contact/contact.html`.

Avoid paths like `C:/myimage.jpg`. They only work on your own computer; once the site is uploaded, the image breaks. Keep images in your website folder and use relative paths such as `images/logo.jpg`.
To link from contact.html back up to the home page, use `../Index.html`. Two dots mean ‘go up one folder’.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Links use text.
href is required and is not displayed.
Same folder: just the file name; subfolder: folder/file.html.
Index.html is the home page.
Good folder organisation makes links work.

diagram.caption: How the files are organised inside your area.

pages.spec: Use the div tag as a container to build a navigation bar
pages.summary: A <div> (division) is a container that groups other elements into a section. Putting all your links inside one div creates a navbar that can be styled as one block.

blocks.text: The `<div>` (**division**) tag is a really versatile element. It is a **container** for other HTML elements: it defines a section of the page. On its own it does not look like anything, but it lets you group things and style them together.
We use a div to build a **navigation bar** (navbar) along the top of the screen by nesting the hyperlinks inside it.

blocks.title: Index.html with a navbar
blocks.code:
Home Page Hobbies Contact

This is going to be your homepage of your website
blocks.output: Three links, ‘Home Page’, ‘Hobbies’ and ‘Contact’, in a row at the top, then the paragraph underneath.

items: The `<div>` opens before the first link and closes after the last one.
The three `<a>` tags are **nested** inside the div, so they are tabbed in one more level.
Copy the same div onto every page so the menu is identical everywhere (consistent navigation).

blocks.text: Remember to use the **Tab** key to indent your tags, so you can see at a glance which links are inside the div.
Modern HTML5 also has a `<nav>` tag made specially for navigation bars. It works just like a div but tells browsers and screen readers ‘this is the menu’.

blocks.title: Worked example: linking all the pages
blocks.context: Create and link all of your pages together (Index, Hobbies, Contact) so you can get from any page to any other.
steps: Put the same navbar div at the top of Index.html and Hobbies.html (same folder, so hrefs are Index.html, Hobbies.html, Contact/contact.html).
contact.html is one folder deeper, so its navbar must go up a level: `../Index.html`, `../Hobbies.html`, and `contact.html` for itself.
Open each page in the browser and click every link to test it.
blocks.answer: Every page has a working navbar; contact.html uses ../ to reach the pages in the folder above.

pages.spec: Compare inline styling, the style tag and external style sheets
pages.summary: CSS controls how a page looks. You can style one tag inline, style one page with a <style> tag in the head, or style a whole site with an external .css file linked in the head.

blocks.text: Styling is why websites look so different from each other even though they use the same tags. It changes colours and fonts, adds shadows and can even add hover effects and animations. Styling is written in [[CSS]] (Cascading Style Sheets).

head: Method
Where the CSS goes
Best for
rows: In a `style` attribute on one tag
Tiny one-off changes; **not** recommended for large projects
Small sites, or styling used on only one page
A separate **.css** file linked from the `<head>`
Large projects: one file styles every page
blocks.caption: Three ways to add styling

blocks.text: 1. Inline styling

blocks.title: Inline style
blocks.output: ‘Heading Text’ in green on a yellow background.

blocks.text: It fits on one line, which seems handy, but it is one of the worst ways to style: you would have to repeat it on every heading on every page. Only use it for small styling that is not repeated anywhere else.
2. The style tag

blocks.code:
Heading Text

Some text about the topic.

Another Heading

Another paragraph on a new topic.
blocks.output: Both ‘Heading Text’ and ‘Another Heading’ are green on yellow.

blocks.text: The style applies to **all** `<h1>` tags on that page, not just one. But to style other pages you would have to copy it into each one.
3. External style sheet

Some text about the topic.

items: A `<link>` tag in the `<head>` tells the browser where to find the styling.
The CSS is laid out just as in the `<style>` tag, but saved as a **.css** file (not .txt).
With `href="myFancyStylesheet.css"` the CSS file must be saved **in the same folder** as the HTML page (or you must give the path to it).
Change one line in the .css file and every linked page updates. This is how professional websites are made.

blocks.title: Key points
items: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how a page looks.
Inline: style attribute on one tag – avoid for big projects.
<style> tag in the head styles one whole page.
External .css linked with <link rel="stylesheet" href="…"> styles every page.
External style sheets are used for professional sites.

check.why: One .css file styles every page.

check.why: Style and link tags go in the head.

check.q: What does CSS stand for?
check.why: Cascading Style Sheets.

practice.q: Describe the **three** ways to add CSS styling to a web page.
practice.a: Inline styling using a style attribute in a tag (1); a <style> tag in the head of the page (1); an external .css style sheet linked using a <link> tag (1).

practice.q: Give **two** advantages of using an external style sheet.
practice.a: Can be used across all the pages of a website (1); to change a style you only change it in one place (1); keeps HTML tidy (1). Any two.

pages.spec: Use tag and class selectors in CSS to style chosen elements
pages.summary: A CSS selector chooses which tags to style. A tag selector (h1) styles every tag of that type; a comma lists several; a class selector (.name) styles only elements with that class.

blocks.text: A [[CSS selector]] is the part of a CSS rule that chooses **which tags you want to style**. After it come curly brackets `{ }` holding the **properties** and **values**, each ending in a semicolon.

blocks.title: The pattern of a CSS rule

head: Selector
Example
What it styles
rows: Only elements with `class="house"` (starts with a full stop)
blocks.caption: Tag and class selectors

blocks.title: Worked example: styling your John Smith page
blocks.context: Link the stylesheet into the head of your John Smith page and add the rule h2 { background: gold; color: tomato; }. What does the page look like now?
steps: In myFancyStylesheet.css add the h2 rule and save it as .css in the same folder.
Refresh the browser: every `<h2>` heading now has a gold background with tomato-red text. Nothing else changes, because the selector only picks `<h2>` tags.
blocks.answer: All h2 headings appear tomato-red on gold. (Does it look great? Red on gold is bright but not very easy to read: remember the colour-scheme rules!)

blocks.title: myFancyStylesheet.css
JohnSmith.html
blocks.code:
John Smith

My Hobbies

I am in the blue house.

This paragraph has no class, so it keeps the normal style.
blocks.output: ‘John Smith’ in red (Arial); ‘My Hobbies’ tomato on gold (Arial); the first paragraph white on navy; the second paragraph plain.

blocks.text: CSS uses American spelling: `color`, not `colour`. If you write `colour: red;` the browser ignores the line.
Forgot a semicolon or curly bracket? The rule after it may stop working. If styling suddenly breaks, check your punctuation first.

Your unit assessment is a test based on an **ERGS houses website**. You can open and edit the site in Notepad or Notepad++ during the test, but you write answers on paper and cannot use the internet, so make sure you know these tags and selectors.

Tag selector: h1 { } styles every h1.
Separate several selectors with commas: h1, h2 { }.
Class selector starts with a dot: .house { } styles class="house".
Properties end with semicolons; spell color the American way.

glossary.def: A global network of interconnected computers: the hardware that lets them communicate.
The huge collection of websites, web pages and resources that we access through the internet.
One screen or document of a website.
A word or image you click on to go to another web page.
A program such as Chrome or Firefox that reads HTML files and displays them as web pages.
The unique address of a web page, e.g. https://www.bbc.co.uk.
The small set of colours (usually 3–5) used consistently throughout a design.
How users move around a website, mainly using menus and links.
The group of people a website or product is designed for.
HyperText Markup Language: the language of tags used to create web pages.

An HTML instruction written in angle brackets, e.g.

; most come in opening and closing pairs.

An opening tag, its content and its closing tag together, e.g.

Hello

.
Extra information inside an opening tag that changes what the tag does, e.g. href or src.
The <head> section of an HTML page, holding information for the browser such as the title; it is not displayed.
The <body> section of an HTML page, holding everything that is displayed.
Using the Tab key to push nested tags in, so it is clear which tags are inside which.
A tag with no closing tag because it has no content, e.g. .
An <li> element: one item in an ordered (<ol>) or unordered (<ul>) list.
The attribute in an <a> tag that gives the link's destination.
The first page of a website, usually saved as index.html.
A link that gives a file's location compared with the current page, e.g. Contact/contact.html.
The <div> (division) tag: a container that groups elements into a section of the page.
A row of links, usually across the top of every page, used to move around a site; a navbar.
Cascading Style Sheets: the language that controls how web pages look, e.g. colours and fonts.
CSS written in a style attribute on a single tag.
A separate .css file of styling, linked from the head of each page so one file styles the whole site.
The part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements to style, e.g. h1 or .house.
A CSS selector starting with a full stop, e.g. .house, that styles only elements with that class.
